title: Matrix: Set Matrix Zeroes
oneLiner: Wherever a cell is 0, zero its whole row and column, using the first row and column as the markers so no extra memory is needed.
keyTakeaway: Don't zero cells while you scan, or new zeros spread further. First record which rows and columns contain a 0, then zero them. Sets of rows and columns cost O(n + m); storing the marks in row 0 and column 0 themselves, plus one flag for whether column 0 itself must be cleared, makes it O(1).
explanation:
Given an m by n matrix, if a cell is 0, set its entire row and its entire column to 0. Do it in place and return the matrix. [[1, 1, 1], [1, 0, 1], [1, 1, 1]] becomes [[1, 0, 1], [0, 0, 0], [1, 0, 1]].

The tempting one-pass approach is wrong: if you zero row 1 and column 1 the moment you see the 0, the next cells you read in that row are now zeros you created, and they wipe out more rows and columns. Separate finding from writing. Pass 1 records every row and every column that contains an original 0. Pass 2 sets matrix[r][c] = 0 whenever row r or column c was recorded. With two sets that is O(m · n) time and O(m + n) space, and it is a perfectly good first answer.

The follow-up asks for O(1) space. Use the matrix's own first row and first column as the record: when matrix[r][c] is 0, set matrix[r][0] = 0 and matrix[0][c] = 0. The corner cell matrix[0][0] can only mean one thing, so let it mark row 0, and keep a separate flag, firstColZero, for column 0. Then zero the inner cells (r >= 1, c >= 1) whose row or column marker is 0, and only after that clear row 0 (if matrix[0][0] is 0) and column 0 (if firstColZero). Clearing the markers last is what keeps them readable.

Both versions read each cell a constant number of times: O(m · n) time. The visualization runs the marker version on a 4 by 4 matrix.

visualizationSteps.message: Zero the rows and columns of every 0. Row 0 and column 0 will hold the markers; firstColZero records column 0 separately.
Found 0 at (1, 1): mark row 1 by setting matrix[1][0] = 0 and column 1 by setting matrix[0][1] = 0.
Found 0 at (3, 3): mark row 3 by setting matrix[3][0] = 0 and column 3 by setting matrix[0][3] = 0.
Zero every inner cell whose row marker or column marker is 0. The markers themselves are still intact.
Last, row 0 and column 0 themselves: matrix[0][0] is not 0, so row 0 keeps its other values, and firstColZero is false, so column 0 does too. The markers written there were already correct zeros.

recognitionSignals: An update that depends on the original values but is written into the same grid: record first, write second.
"In place, constant extra space" for a grid: reuse a row or column of the grid as scratch memory.
gotchas: Zeroing during the scan lets your own zeros trigger more zeroing.
matrix[0][0] cannot mark both row 0 and column 0; one of them needs its own flag.
Clearing the first row or column before using them as markers destroys the record; do them last.
confusableWith: Game of Life has the same "don't overwrite what you still need to read" problem; it solves it by encoding old and new state in each cell.
Number of Islands spreads from a cell to its neighbours; here a zero affects whole rows and columns, not neighbours.

complexity.note: Two passes over the n · m cells. The marker version keeps its record inside the first row and column plus one flag, O(1) extra; the simpler version with a set of rows and a set of columns is O(n + m), also a fine answer.
